title: Day 4: Babies K, L, M, N, O & P

blocks.text: 6 July 2023
Judge's Summing Up Day 4: Babies K, L, M, N, O & P
CONTENTS
SUMMING-UP (continued)
Housekeeping
Thursday, 6 July 2023
(In the presence of the jury)
SUMMING-UP (continued)

When we adjourned yesterday afternoon I had reminded you about [Baby K]'s clinical condition following her birth at 02.12 on the morning of 17 February, which was essentially normal, good, although she was very premature, and her having been given surfactant, albeit late, and having been commenced on an intravenous dextrose infusion.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The swipe data reproduced on tile 63 in her sequence of events records that Joanne Williams, who you'll recall was her designated nurse, left the neonatal unit at 03.47, so about an hour and a half after [Baby K] was born. She said that she went to visit [Baby K]'s parents to update them and would not have left [Baby K] unless she was stable and was with other members of staff. She was quite stable.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Dr Jayaram said that he and Nurse Williams were happy that [Baby K] was stable and settled and a morphine infusion had started. Tile 50 relates to the intensive care chart recording that at 03.50 [Baby K] was given a bolus of morphine sulphate.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: If you go to the second page in section 14 of your second jury bundle -- that's the reference, I'm not suggesting you do, that's where it is, there are paper documents there -- you have the neonatal intensive care chart for the relevant time and it shows the commencement of a morphine infusion at 03.30 and a bolus at 03.50. That was not, said Joanne Williams, in her handwriting. However, behind tile 69 is an infusion chart with an entry for 17 February at 2016 at 03.50, being for an infusion beginning at that time.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Joanne Williams accepted in cross-examination that the infusion could have started at 03.50 after an initial bolus had been given.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Dr Jayaram said Joanne Williams had told him the defendant was babysitting for her. He said that at this point they were aware
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: of unexpected events and the association of the defendant with them. He felt extremely uncomfortable. He was in the corridor opposite nurseries 2 and 3, at a desk round the corner from nursery 1, writing notes he thought.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: After 2 to 2.5 minutes, he got up from the desk just to check on [Baby K] and to prove to himself that he wasn't being ridiculous and irrational. He went into nursery 1, through the door that's not marked on our plan, and as he walked up, he saw the defendant standing by [Baby K]'s ventilator at the top end. She didn't have her hands in the incubator. Then he looked up at the monitor and saw that [Baby K]'s saturations were dropping.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: They were in the 80s and they continued to drop.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The ventilator wasn't alarming. The monitor, which is usually set to alarm when the saturations drop below 90%, wasn't alarming either. He recalled saying, "What's happening?" She looked and said words along the lines of, "She's having a desaturation". He could see [Baby K]'s chest, which had been moving with the breaths from the ventilator, but it was no longer moving.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The ventilator was still delivering breaths. He disconnected the ventilator from the ET tube, tested the tube and ascertained that it was not working as it should be, but it wasn't blocked, though he didn't recall looking in the tube to see if there was a blockage. As soon as he ventilated [Baby K] with Neopuffs through a face mask, her chest started moving and her sats picked up.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Dr Jayaram said usually babies will maintain saturations for 30 to 60 seconds before they start desaturating, so for her saturations to have been in the 80s and dropping he inferred that something had happened at least 30 to 60 seconds before he walked in.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Dr Smith remembered coming back in the room, having been out briefly, and saw Dr Jayaram on the right-hand side of the incubator as he walked in. The ventilator was disconnected and [Baby K] was being given breaths through a Neopuff. He reintubated [Baby K] with a 2.5 millimetre tube, measuring 6.5 from the lips, after giving her a bolus of morphine and reconnecting the ventilator on basically the same settings.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Joanne Williams, on returning, remembered walking back into the unit and hearing the red alarm sound from nursery 1. She thought Caroline Oakley and the defendant were in the nursery. She helped with the re-intubation and noted that air entry was clear and equal and a large amount of bloodstained oral secretions, which now she had no recollection of but would have been
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: something to be aware of and are sometimes not uncommon with multiple intubations. Her oxygen saturations were down to 40% and she was not improving.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Caroline Oakley has no recollection of the desaturation. After [Baby K] had been stabilised, Dr Jayaram asked Caroline Oakley how this had happened.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: She said to him she thought that the ET tube was secure but she wasn't there. She said tubes can be dislodged with movement and she didn't have a lot of experience of babies of 25 weeks' gestation. A UVC was inserted but they were not able to insert a UAC.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Dr Smith confirmed that doctors have knowledge of how to adjust the settings on ventilators, but the actual connection of all the pipes from the ventilator to the baby is done by the nurses. The doctor would still be close by, just to supervise and be on hand if the baby needed re-intubating, for example, but the actual connection is done by the nurses.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Stuart Eccles gave evidence that was agreed about the monitors in use in the unit, stating that monitors on the neonatal unit automatically default to neonatal settings, which cannot be changed. If the baby's monitor readings go outside of the set range it triggers an audible alarm. It is possible to deactivate the alarms on the Philips MP3 neonatal monitor for 1 minute using the alarm pause button on the touchscreen. This will then give a visible countdown display on top of the screen. Once the 1 minute has expired, the alarms will reactivate. If the user wants to further silence the alarm, they can press the alarm pause button again, which will give a further 1 minute of alarm silence, but this can't happen until the previous 1 minute has expired. If the user presses the pause alarm button again within the 1 minute time frame the alarm will no longer be paused and will begin to sound again.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Dr Jayaram's account of events was challenged in crossexamination. He was asked why he didn't confront the defendant at the time. He said it was his job to deal with [Baby K] and to notice patterns and raise concerns and this was added to the list of concerns that he and his colleagues had already noticed in relation to the association of the defendant with unusual events.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: They wanted to have this investigated but were unclear as to how to get that done.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It's not appropriate, he said, to document suspicions in clinical notes. He did put in a Datix report but concerns had been raised by Dr Brearey to senior executive level medical
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: management in February and, after this incident, he said they were raised again. As clinicians, they put their faith in the system, in senior management, to guide them how to escalate concerns and investigate them. They were told, that's the clinicians, that it was unlikely that anything was going on and to see what happens.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: In retrospect, he wished they had bypassed management and gone to the police and put in a Datix form. He was referred to the network service report in relation to transporting [Baby K] to Alder Hey, which recorded at 05.55:
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: "Call received from Dr Jayaram. Baby dislodged the tube and had to be re-intubated."
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: He could not remember what he had said and had not seen that note, but it was highly unlikely at her age that she had dislodged the tube herself.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: When shown the morphine infusion chart, he accepted that his note at the time that she had been sedated did not accord with the charts, but denied that he had deliberately shifted his evidence to emphasise that [Baby K] was sedated at the time the tube became dislodged.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: He repeated that she was not making any purposeful movements at that time. He also refuted the suggestion that he had picked up the time that Joanne Williams had left the nursery and worked that into his account, implicitly building a case against the defendant and changed things as he'd gone along.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: He said he'd never seen the swipe data or known the specific timings. He accepted that things could have been done better, but said he was not trying to distract everyone from what was suggested to be a poor level of care by creating this issue and bolstering suspicion against the defendant.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The decision for [Baby K] to be born at the Countess of Chester, which you'll remember was one of the criticisms that was made, was, he said, made by paediatricians, which it was.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: When interviewed about [Baby K] on 5 July 2018, the defendant said she recalled [Baby K] only because she was a tiny baby and was 25 weeks' gestation and the Countess of Chester would not usually have babies of [Baby K]'s age and weight on the unit. She did not remember the ET tube slipping, nor did she remember any subsequent collapses during the remainder of the shift.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: In the interview on 12 June 2019, she was informed that Joanne Williams was [Baby K]'s designated nurse. She agreed that she thought Joanne Williams would not have left [Baby K] to update
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: the parents unless [Baby K] was stable and her ET tube was correctly positioned. She did not remember being left alone with [Baby K] in nursery 1 or being at [Baby K]'s cot side or [Baby K]'s saturations falling. She could not remember whether the alarm was silent, although she agreed it should have been sounding if [Baby K]'s saturations had fallen into the 80s.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: She denied dislodging [Baby K]'s ET tube and had no recollection of the tube slipping and said she would have raised the alarm when Dr Jayaram had walked in if she had seen the saturations dropping or the tube had slipped.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: She thought it possible that she was waiting to see if [Baby K] self-corrected and explained that nurses didn't always intervene straightaway if levels were not "dangerously low".
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: In her evidence to you, in answer to her counsel, the defendant confirmed that she didn't have an independent recollection of [Baby K] on the unit, but did recall seeing her at one point because it was unusual to have a baby of 25 weeks' gestation. She denied interfering with [Baby K]'s tube at any time. There wasn't a time when she was in the nursery and Dr Jayaram came in to find her standing there close to [Baby K]. She did not recall an incident where she was present when [Baby K] desaturated and Dr Jayaram was involved at about 3.50 or any other time.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: She referred to the neonatal review and said that she was doing obs and feeding GT, one of her babies in nursery 2, at 03.30; that's lines 115 and 116 and J30494. She also referred to J30497, GT's feeding chart, which recorded a bottle was offered and 55ml was given and the nappy was changed. She said this could take half an hour and the shortest time would be 20 minutes, it could take up to an hour.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: When cross-examined, she agreed that Joanne Williams, [Baby K]'s designated nurse in nursery 1, had left and that the swipe data showed her leaving at 03.47, tile 63. There was also evidence that Dr Jayaram was speaking to someone from the transport service at 03.41, tile 59, and there were phones at the nurses' station. She had no recollection of [Baby K] desaturating when Dr Jayaram walked in when she was standing over [Baby K], so she could not confirm or deny it or whether [Baby K] was desaturating at that time or whether the alarm was sounding.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: She did say that if she had seen [Baby K] desaturating, she would have waited to see if she self-corrected. She didn't believe the event did happen. She had no direct memory of it. She accepted that the morphine infusion had been running since 03.50.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: She said that although she had no memory of this event, if a baby of [Baby K]'s gestation and condition had been desaturating she would simply have waited, maybe 10 or 20 seconds, to see if she self-corrected. She knew that was common practice in the neonatal unit in Chester and Liverpool Women's Hospital, to wait and see if the baby self-corrected, if they are not at a lifethreatening level.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The agreed evidence of Elizabeth Morgan, a nursing adviser, was that in her professional experience it is possible for an ET tube to become dislodged in an unsedated or active baby or where securing ties have become loose and it is very unlikely a nurse would leave the bedside of an intubated neonate unless they were very confident the ET tube was correctly positioned and secure, the baby was inactive, and they'd only be away briefly and had informed a colleague who would attend the baby if an alarm should sound.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It was also her professional experience that when observing a falling oxygen saturation level in a baby of this age and gestation, it would be standard good nursing practice to immediately attend the bedside to actively observe the baby, ascertain any cause for changes in oxygen levels, and to take corrective action, calling for help to alert other members of staff of the situation if necessary.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: A series of checks would be carried out immediately to ascertain why the oxygen levels had dropped. For example, has the tube become blocked or dislodged? Has the baby developed a pneumothorax or has there been an equipment failure? She did not believe that it would be normal nursing practice to wait and see if the baby self-corrected at this gestational age given the lungs are so immature and the risks associated with unplanned extubation.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: At 06.15, it was noted that [Baby K]'s saturations began to drop and the indications were that it was a problem with ventilation. [Baby K] was extubated again.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: She responded to ventilation via a mask and a new 2.5 millimetre ET tube was put into the same length.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: She was settled for the next 30 minutes. Then, at around 07.25, [Nurse B], who was going to take over as shift leader for the day shift, was at the nurses' station at that time before the handover when she received a call for help from the defendant, who was at the side of the [Baby K]'s incubator.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: [Nurse B] entered the nursery behind Dr Jayaram and Joanne Williams. [Baby K] was having bradycardia and a desaturation and the defendant was Neopuffing her via her ET tube. Dr Jayaram's
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: note behind tile 106 sets out the details. [Baby K]'s blood pressure dropped and, despite a saline bolus, her heart rate suddenly dropped to less than 100 beats per minute.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It was noted that her tube was not in the same place as it had been, it was too far in, and was adjusted back to its appropriate place or position. She was taken off the ventilator and ventilated with the T-piece through the Neopuff down the ET tube. Cardiac compressions were started. She was re-intubated and she settled again.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: [Nurse B] stayed with Melanie Taylor, who was then her designated nurse for that day shift, to assist with all the infusions [Baby K] needed during the course of the rest of the morning.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Dr Jayaram had rung NWTS, the hospital transfer service, at 03.15, about an hour after [Baby K] was born.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The advice was to stabilise [Baby K]. The transport team arrived at about 09.00 and responsibility was handed over to them, both teams being responsible for her care, the transport team being a specialised team.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Dr Kamalanathan, a consultant neonatal paediatrician at Arrowe Park Hospital, received the handover. The UVC was low-lying but acceptable for the purpose of transfer. [Baby K] needed multiple medications to get her blood pressure up. Her oxygen levels couldn't be maintained within normal limits. Nitric oxide was introduced to her ventilation circuit to make the blood vessels in the lungs dilate, or enlarge, to help the lungs get oxygen.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: [Baby K] left the Countess of Chester, having been stabilised by the transport team, at 12.50. The prosecution say [Baby K] was a settled baby who could not dislodge her own tube and it was dislodged.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Dr Babarao, who had been a consultant neonatologist since 2013, and specialises in treating babies from 22 weeks' gestation, and was also a consultant in neonatal transport with the transport team in 2016, was the consultant with responsibility for [Baby K] upon her arrival at Arrowe Park.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: She arrived there at 13.15. Her condition continued to deteriorate. X-rays showed she had severe lung disease. Infection was not an issue. There was no record of dislodgement of her ET tube at Arrowe Park.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Her blood pressure got worse and she was receiving the maximum amounts of medication and her sats were low.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: In the early hours of 20 February, after discussion with her parents, the decision was made to stop [Baby K]'s intensive care, her ET tube was removed at 05.10, and [Baby K] died at 05.28.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The cause of death was certified as (1A), extreme prematurity, (2) severe respiratory distress syndrome.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Dr Babarao agreed that the outcome for [Baby K] may have been better if she had been born at a tertiary centre and that it was originally intended that she should be born in one, but it was unclear to him why she was not and may have been due to a shortage of maternity beds in Arrowe Park.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: He was also asked about the golden hour, which is the initial hour after birth of a preterm baby, to give them the best possible next few hours and outcomes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It is good practice, not strict guidelines, that certain things have to be implemented within the hour. The key is to do the most essential things in the first few hours, let the baby settle, and take some time and then increase support as the baby needs.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: He said that if intubating a neonate, surfactant should be given as soon as possible after intubation.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Antibiotics should be given within the first hour.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: At the time of the golden practice, an umbilical line should be inserted in the first hour. However, Dr Babarao said neonatologists have now moved away from that and a peripheral cannula, which [Baby K] had, was equally enough. He said that her death wasn't avoidable because she was extremely sick right from the beginning.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: However, looking at the overall picture, had her care been optimal, her death was potentially avoidable, the main factor being her in utero transfer from the Countess of Chester to a level 3 perinatal or neonatal centre. That would have improved her outcomes as an extreme preterm baby. But as you know, it couldn't be done, and the advice from the tertiary hospital was that she should stay there and she should be born there.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: When further interviewed on 10 November 2020, the defendant said she had no recollection of [Baby K]'s tube slipping at 07.30 on 17 February and suggested that maybe the tube had not been secured properly. She agreed that she searched for the name [Surname of Baby K] on Facebook on 20 April 2018, but could not remember having done so.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: She explained that in her text messaging later she was complaining that the unit had been understaffed at the time of [Baby K]'s admission.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: In her evidence she said she had nothing to do with the events at 06.15 and 07.25. She agreed that [Baby K] had been on a morphine infusion since 03.50 and that in order to create the computer note relating to her admission record at tile 104, which was created at 06.04 and closed at 06.10, she will have had to get [Baby K]'s medical notes from her incubator and return them there.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: She could not dispute or agree with [Nurse B]'s evidence of being at [Baby K]'s incubator and calling her in to nursery 1 at 07.25.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: At 06.49 she was updating the computer in relation to GT's, her baby, administration history, and at 07.00 she was making entries relating to another baby, AR, both GT and AR being in nursery 2. She agreed she had no reason to be in nursery 1 at 07.25.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: In relation to her Facebook search on 20 April 2018, she said she was looking because:
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: "You still think of patients you cared for."
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Her only recollection now of caring for [Baby K] was giving the morphine infusion at 03.50. From memory now, she could not think of a reason. Nothing out of the ordinary happened that night. It was a busy shift, that was all she could say about it.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: So the issue, as you have known, in [Baby K]'s case is a factual one. The prosecution accept that they cannot prove the defendant's acts caused her death, she was a very sick baby with obvious breathing difficulties, but allege that the defendant attempted to kill her.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: None of the radiographs, namely the three images taken on 17 February at 06.07, 07.55 and 11.28 respectively, assist in relation to the issues between the prosecution and the defence in her case.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I move on, therefore, to counts 16 and 17, [Baby L] and [Baby M]. At 10.13 on Friday, 8 April 2016, [Mother of Babies L & M], the wife of [Father of Babies L & M], gave birth by caesarean section to twins, [Baby L], referred to in the notes as twin 1, and [Baby M], twin 2. They were 33 weeks and 2 days' gestation.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It had been a routine pregnancy until March.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: [Mother of Babies L & M] was then admitted to hospital for 2 weeks before the semi-selective caesarean section. Twin 1, [Baby L], did not appear to be growing at the correct rate.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The birth went well. Both babies were born in good condition and did not require breathing support in theatre, both weighed about 3 pounds. The defendant, who was working a day shift that day and the next, was present at their birth, as was Dr Bhowmik, then a registrar.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The twins were admitted to nursery 1 in the unit and the defendant was [Baby L]'s designated nurse for the rest of that day shift. This, as you know, is a second case in which the prosecution allege a baby, wholly and inappropriately and without medical approval, was given unprescribed manufactured insulin. It is alleged that the defendant attempted to kill [Baby L] by putting insulin into bags of dextrose solution, the first of which was set up 2 hours after he was born. As is common for premature babies, his blood sugar level was low.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The plasma from a blood sample taken later in the afternoon provided readings that are only explicable on the basis that [Baby L] had been given exogenous insulin.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The infusion from that first bag of 10% dextrose continued until the following day, Saturday, 9 April.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Another bag may have been put up at midday, 12.00 hours, and a new one, with a stronger concentration of dextrose, 12.5%, was put up at 16.30 on 9 April.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: A further bag with a concentration of 15% dextrose was put up at 02.30 or 03.00 on 10 April and yet another was put up at 01.45 on 11 April. I'm going to go back to the chart in relation to this in a moment.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Professor Hindmarsh was of the opinion that the hypoglycaemic event continued from 9 April to about 15.00 hours on 11 April, with the insulin being infused intravenously by way of having been added to the infusion system in several bags that had been made up, which could all have been done at once. That's adding to the infusions.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: On a conservative view, the addition of in the region of 10 units of insulin to a bag would be sufficient to produce the hypoglycaemic effect and also to generate the plasma insulin concentration that was measured in the sample on 9 April. The vials of insulin contain 100 units per millilitre, so 10 units is a tenth of a millilitre, 1% of the volume of a bottle, which would not be noticeable just on a routine stock check and, if added to infusion bags, the addition of one-tenth of a
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: millilitre would not be noticed in a 500ml bag, nor would there be any change in the colour of the bag nor would you see any cloudiness in the bag itself.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Professor Hindmarsh was of the opinion that, depending on how many bags were hung, two or three bags had insulin added to them. If the plastic giving set isn't changed then insulin, being a protein, will stick very nicely to plastic so the giving set as well could potentially have insulin stuck on to the walls of the tubing, from which it could fall off over a period of time as well. He agreed that although sticky insulin could account for some of the insulin being infused from the walls of a previous giving set over time it would require additional insulin to maintain the levels up to 11 April. That's why he said it must have been in a number of bags.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: In [Baby M]'s case, it is alleged that the defendant injected air into his abdomen on the second day of his life, Saturday, 9 April. There is an obvious overlap in the evidence relating to the respective events in their cases, but, as with other cases involving twins, there are separate sequences of events and the evidence has been separated as much as possible. I remind you first of the evidence relating to [Baby L], count 14.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The defendant worked four long day shifts, starting on Wednesday, 6 April to Saturday, 9 April. She told you at that time she had moved into her house and drew attention to messages between her and Sophie Ellis and [Nurse E] on the evening of 8 April at tiles 57 to 63 relating to work and her taking Saturday the 9th as an extra day. The unit was still fairly busy, she said, but not quite as busy as previously.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Dr Bhowmik inserted a peripheral intravenous line into [Baby L]'s left hand at 11.15 on 8 April, an hour after he was born; his clinical note, made at 12.00 hours, midday, is behind tile 12. On admission to the unit, [Baby L] was generally well, being active and alert. His breathing rate was a little bit elevated at 65, but not a concern as it is common for babies born by caesarean section. His weight was low and his blood sugar at 1.9 was a bit low, but this was common for premature babies.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: He was started on intravenous fluids with glucose.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Behind tile 13 is the defendant's nursing note, written as his designated nurse at 17.42. In relation to the low blood sugar, she wrote:
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: "Initial blood sugar shortly after birth 1.9 micromoles. Advised by Reg Bhowmik to commence a 10% glucose at 3ml per kg per hour and give 60ml per kg per day of donor-expressed breast milk. Myself and shift leader A [that's Amy] Davies have discussed
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: this with Reg Bhowmik as does not follow the hypoglycaemic pathway."
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The reference to the hypoglycaemic pathway was to the policy at the Countess of Chester to feed babies with milk before infusing them with dextrose. The decision was for Dr Bhowmik. Amy Davies had no concerns about this. Dr Bhowmik prescribed the dextrose. The infusion therapy prescription sheet is J17948 behind tile 10 and it's the first paper document in section 15 of your second bundle.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Dr Bhowmik wrote out the prescription and the rate of infusion. The first two entries were struck through by him and the third, at a rate of 4.4ml per hour, was the set rate, which was checked by the defendant and Amy Davies, who were responsible for administering it, each of them initialling the sheet.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: In her evidence the defendant confirmed that dextrose bags of concentrations of 10% and 50% were kept in the cupboard in nursery 1 and said insulin was kept in the equipment room. 10% bags were very commonly used and were non-patient specific. She couldn't recall if any were kept under lock and key.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The first infusion started at midday, 12.00 hours, on that Friday, 8 April. It was a 500ml bag of 10% dextrose. The bags would normally be changed every 24 hours unless the concentration of dextrose changed, in which case a new bag would be used. The dextrose solution was then pumped through the giving set and a filter into the cannula that had been inserted by Dr Bhowmik into [Baby L]'s left hand.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Later that afternoon, at 14.35, the defendant and Amy Davies administered antibiotic medication to [Baby L]; tile 30. Amy Davies carried out the regular observations, noting and initialling the results on the observation chart between 10.00 and 18.00; J17987, the sixth page document in section 15.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Amy Davies denied having administered insulin to [Baby L] and was unaware of anyone else doing so. Insulin, she said, would usually only be given to a baby who has two consecutive blood sugars over 12 and is hyperglycaemic. Although it is not a controlled drug, the insulin would have to be prescribed by a doctor.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: In section 6 of your first jury bundle you have a three-page table of blood sugar readings and the times, concentrations, rates and volumes of dextrose administered to [Baby L] from the records from 10.58 on 8 April, 45 minutes after he was born, until 23.00 on 11 April, some two and a half days later. It might be helpful for you to have that to hand because it is a good reference document. There you are, that one.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The first bundle, section 6.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'm going to make some specific reference to some of the entries, but I shall also refer to other things and you can then refer yourselves to that table as I go along as I'm reciting the history of events.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Professor Hindmarsh was asked to look at this case by Dr Evans. This was the 60th case that Dr Evans had been asked to look at and when in the notes he found the result of the plasma test with a very high value of insulin and a low value of C-peptide at 264, when, as you know, the readings should have been the other way around, he suggested, that's Dr Evans suggested to the police, that they should approach a specialist in endocrinology to review his findings.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Professor Hindmarsh told you that newborns and neonates have higher glucose requirements than children and adults and it is generally accepted that any reading of a blood sugar level of under 2.6, or according to some 2.4, millimoles per litre is a cause for concern.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: So it was in keeping with the low reading of 1.9 at 10.58 that an infusion of dextrose had been commenced; the first entry on the chart.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Behind tile 5 -- don't go to it, I'm giving you the reference -you've got a paper copy, which is page 8 in section 15 of your other bundle -- are the blood gas results, which record the figure of 1.9, to which I have just referred as the first entry. You can now follow the readings on that chart.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: At 12.14 to 12.15 it had risen to 2.5 and then at 16.00 it was 5.8, then fell back to 3.3 at 18.10. All those entries were signed for by the defendant on the document behind tile 5.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Tracey Jones, a senior lecturer in nursing and then working as an agency nurse at the Countess of Chester, covered [Baby L] as his designated nurse for the night shift of the 8th/9th. Her note of that shift is behind tile 78. There were no concerns. [Baby L]'s pre-feed blood glucose readings were all above 2 millimoles, as you've seen from the chart, all the readings up to the first thick black line on that first page. Therefore they were to discontinue monitoring as requested by the registrar. The registrar said there's no problem with the readings so you can discontinue having to take them.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The records against the initials of Tracey Jones were that his glucose level was 2 at 20.00 hours and 2.4 at 21.00 hours. No
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: readings of blood sugar levels were recorded after 21.00 because, as I've said, they were told to discontinue.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: However, there are what appear to be recorded blood sugar levels on the fluid balance chart J18031, just above the feeds row of, 2.3 at 21.00 hours, 2.2 at 22.00 and 3.6 at 24.00.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The observation chart behind tile 54 -- you have a paper copy at page 6 -- has Tracey Jones' initialled entries at the bottom of the page following on from those of the defendant's up to 06.00 on 9 April. No fluid bags were changed during the course of Tracey Jones' shift.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Mary Griffith took over from Tracey Jones and was the designated nurse for both [Baby L] and [Baby M] on the day shift of Saturday, 9 April. The defendant was also on that shift, so coming on to the unit at 07.30 for handover and was the nurse responsible for GT and TSB, who were also in nursery 1.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The clinical and nursing personnel on duty that shift are in your neonatal review and behind tile 88.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Belinda Williamson, then Simcock, and Ashleigh Hudson and a nursery nurse, Angela McShane, were the other nursing staff. Mary Griffith said [Baby L] was stable in nursery 1. Behind tile 98 is the nursing note written at the end of the shift.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Towards the back of section 15 in your second bundle you have a paper copy of the fluid balance chart from 01.00 to 24.00 hours on that Saturday, 9 April. That is the document behind tile 97. The next document is the continuation chart for the following day, Sunday, 10 April.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Going back to the table that you have, you will see that the blood sugar readings, which were recommenced at 10.00 hours and which are recorded there, are reproduced below the -- in the bottom quarter of that page. You can see the entry at 10.00 hours.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Professor Hindmarsh's evidence was that [Baby L]'s blood sugar levels on 8 April were low in some cases, but basically acceptable. But by the first reading at 10.00 on 9 April, [Baby L] was hypoglycaemic, so against the 10.00 entry, that is when he is hypoglycaemic, and that insulin must have been added some time after midnight and by 09.30 that morning at the latest.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: He explained it is fairly easy to get insulin into a dextrose infusion by drawing it up in a needle and syringe and inserting it through the portal at the bottom of the bag in the same way that the concentration of dextrose in a bag of 10% concentration
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: is increased by adding some from a 50% concentration bag. You saw the video recording of that process being undertaken.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: For reasons that I reminded you of in [Baby F]'s case, and having regard to the readings, Professor Hindmarsh said that at least three bags must have contained insulin. If the insulin had been infused by individual intravenous boluses to result in the blood sugar readings that were obtained, it would have required between 10 and 12 boluses at least. The bags could all have had insulin added to them at the same time, he said. A very small quantity of insulin was required. As I have said to you, it is 1% of a 10ml bottle of insulin added to a -- one-tenth of a millilitre added to a 500ml bag. Once in the dextrose bag, it would not be known that it was there from either smell or from appearance.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The agreed evidence of Karen Morris read to you was that in 2015 and 2016 Actrapid was the only insulin used in the unit at the Countess of Chester. It's a fast-acting insulin and came in a 10ml vial, which contained 100ml a unit. This is also relevant evidence relating back to the case of [Baby F]. You will remember I said I would come on to the other evidence relating to insulin when I came to [Baby L]'s case.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: At that time a member of the pharmacy team would attend the unit once a week on a Friday and assess what amounts of stock drugs, which included insulin, were required. They would then replenish the unit's stocks later that day. Alternatively, unit staff could complete a stock requisition book, requesting extra if they needed it. They no longer have any of those paper records. The reports show that in 2014 a total of three vials of Actrapid were issued: one in January, one in April and one in November.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: In 2015, a total of six vials were issued: one in May, one in August, and two in both October and November.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: In 2016, two vials were issued: one in April and one in July.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Mary Griffith said it was quite a shock when the blood sugar level dropped after the increase in volume of dextrose at 10.00 hours, the reading taken at 12.00 hours being 1.6 pre-feed. So at that time the volume of dextrose was increased to 3ml per kilogram.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The defendant in evidence said she couldn't assist with why there was a low reading at that time. She had nothing to do with insulin and the bags.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Mary Griffith was not prepared to say that the bag was changed at 12 midday. The volume was increased and she agreed that when
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: it was put to her that the bags -- but she agreed when it was put to her that bags were normally changed every 24 hours.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The defendant said a new bag was commenced at that time by them. The defendant said she had nothing to do with the bags before then and couldn't explain the reading at 12.00 hours.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Mary Griffith said she also took a blood sample by way of a heel prick. This was some time after 12.00.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: She could not remember the exact time but she wrote in her notes that after the rate was increased to 3ml per kilogram:
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: "Blood sugar 1 hour later, 1.6. Blood taken for lab but due to emergency, not podded at once."
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Podding was placing the sample in a plastic pod for putting into the air-driven system or chute, sending it straight to the lab. She said she gave the sample to someone for podding and that the emergency was the collapse of [Baby M], which was at about 16.00. She was making up a 12.5% dextrose bag for [Baby L] when [Baby M]'s alarm went off and he collapsed. The defendant went over to him.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: You'll recall the playing of the video, to which I have already referred, about the process that is undertaken when a 12.5% bag is made up, adding dextrose from a 50% bag.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The blood sample was labelled as having been taken at 15.35 hours. The evidence therefore is that it was taken some time after the recorded blood sugar of 1.6 at 12.00 and the labelling at 15.35.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Mary Griffith went to help with the resuscitation of [Baby M] and the doctors arrived soon after and she handed over responsibility for [Baby L] to Belinda Williamson.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The only time that [Baby L]'s dextrose bag was changed, said Mary Griffith, was when the new bag with 12.5% dextrose was put up, which was after the blood sample had been taken.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The blood sample labelled as having been taken at 15.35 on 9 April for testing of insulin and C-peptide levels was received at the Royal Liverpool Hospital at 15.47 on 11 April. Had there been any mislabelling, Dr Anna Milan told you the sample would have been rejected and no analysis would have been undertaken.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: She confirmed all the quality control testing processes that are carried out in relation to the equipment before and after samples are analysed and the standard operating procedures and
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: performance checks were carried out by the Royal Liverpool in relation to [Baby L]'s sample.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Reference was also made to external quality assessment routinely carried out by the United Kingdom Laboratory Accreditation Service, which, explained the scheme director of that service, Dr Gwen Wark, a highly qualified clinical biochemist, sends out a variety of samples to laboratories for testing, which they have already tested, every 6 weeks without them, that's the hospital laboratories, knowing that the service is the source of the request. The accreditation service then compares their results. The laboratories have two targets to achieve.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Dr Wark produced four reports: two covering the period relating to the testing of [Baby F]'s sample and two covering the period of [Baby L]'s sample. All results fell within the required targets. Dr Wark said that, based on the records in their laboratory in Surrey, in terms of accuracy and efficiency, the laboratory at the Royal Liverpool was performing very well in relation to the required criteria of testing.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: In short, there is no evidence to doubt the reliability of the test results, you may think.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: [Baby L]'s sample provided readings of 264 picomoles per litre for C-peptide and 1,099 picomoles per litre for insulin. The results are set out in J26995 and J26996, of which you have paper copies in the back of section 15. They were sent to the Countess of Chester who were alerted to a problem. As Dr Milan explained and Dr Gibbs and Professor Hindmarsh, those results were the wrong way round. I remind you again that normally your C-peptide should be five to ten times higher than the insulin if it's insulin and C-peptide that you have made yourself.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Dr Gibbs said that as his insulin level was 1,099, [Baby L]'s Cpeptide level should have been somewhere between 5,000 and 10,000; in fact it was 264. So there was far more insulin than C-peptide, which is a reverse of the normal situation. This meant that most of the insulin in [Baby L]'s blood was manufactured synthetic insulin, which does not have C-peptide associated with it, and it had been given to him and was therefore exogenous insulin. [Baby L] had not had prescribed synthetic insulin and it would have been totally inappropriate to do so. To give it to someone was dangerous.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Both the insulin and C-peptide results were rung through by a colleague of Dr Milan, Dr Sarah Davies, to the consultant medic in the biochemistry laboratory at the Countess of Chester with the comment:
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: "Difficult to interpret without the concurrent glucose but if the patient was hypoglycaemic at the time it's a very inappropriate set of results."
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: [Baby L] was indeed hypoglycaemic. Dr Milan was not aware of anything that gave her any concern as to the accuracy of the results. She was asked in cross-examination about the possible effect on the stability of the sample if it was not stored properly and a possible failure to spin the sample to remove the cells or chill or freeze it as quickly as should be the norm. She explained that in the case of insulin, the consequence is the reading is more likely to go down, so if the sample had not been treated appropriately, the true insulin level could have been even higher than the recorded result. C-peptide is very stable, having a much longer half-life.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Professor Hindmarsh confirmed this was the case.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: A delay of 6 hours would -- so the reading itself was a minimum rather than a maximum.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Dr John Gibbs, referring to results of the analysis and the results on J18025 and J18026 behind tile 190, also confirmed that a low growth hormone, which can cause low blood sugar level, was not the cause in [Baby L]'s case and this was confirmed by Professor Hindmarsh. The cause for the hypoglycaemia was the exogenous administration of insulin.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: In her first police interview, the defendant explained [Baby L]'s low blood sugar levels were not a huge surprise. Additional glucose and/or feeding would usually resolve the issue. She confirmed her signatures on the charts and agreed that she had had significant involvement in his care. She said a neonate would only be given insulin in the event of high blood sugar levels. She said very prolonged low blood sugar levels can cause brain damage and even death. It wasn't a common thing to have a baby on insulin, but there were babies on insulin. She had completed a competency framework and they had the hypoglycaemia pathway policy on the unit.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Although insulin was kept in a locked fridge on the unit in the equipment room, the keys were simply passed between registered nurses and nursery nurses. There was no record of who had the keys or a requirement to keep a log of what was removed unless they were controlled drugs.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Any addition to an infusion bag was very rare.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It would be added using a syringe via the port in the bag itself and would have to be prescribed by a doctor.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: She confirmed her signatures on the infusion therapy chart behind tile 115. She denied having deliberately administered insulin to [Baby L] and did not believe that a mistake could have been made by administering the wrong medication with two people signing for the drug.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: When it was suggested that the insulin was a deliberate act of sabotage, she replied, "That wasn't done by me". She didn't know how insulin could be given accidentally and said that if used inappropriately, it would cause hypoglycaemia. She thought an explanation for insulin in [Baby L]'s circulation was that it had been in one of the bags or the fluids he was already receiving and she denied responsibility for that.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Based on this evidence, the prosecution say there is incontrovertible evidence that, like [Baby F], [Baby L] was given manufactured insulin and that must have been done at some time prior to the blood sample being taken at 15.35 on Saturday, 9 April and the readings indicate it must have been before the 10.00 hours reading of 1.9 that day.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Their case is that insulin was added to the bag of dextrose that had been hung at midday on 8 April, the first bag, early in the shift of the 9th, and resulted in the analysis of the blood sample that was taken at 15.35 on 9 April and accounted for the blood sugar levels remaining persistently low from 10.00 hours, despite the dextrose infusions. This, they say, was done by the defendant when she was on shift.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The issue, therefore, is who was responsible and what they did by causing exogenous insulin to be administered to a newly born baby who was hypoglycaemic.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The other nurses on duty in the unit over the relevant period, Tracey Jones, Mary Griffith, Belinda Williamson, [Nurse B], Bernadette Butterworth, Valerie Thomas, Minna Lappalainen, Clare Bevan, Ashleigh Hudson and Lisa Walker all say they did not administer any insulin to [Baby L] and were unaware of any being administered.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Despite the increased administration of dextrose on the afternoon of 9 April, and I'm looking at the first page of the chart, at a concentration of 12.5%, [Baby L]'s blood sugar levels remained low. [Dr A] was on duty on the night of the 9th to 10 April. His notes at midnight behind tile 226 record that during his night review [Baby L]'s blood glucose levels were falling and he assumed he was called because falling levels can cause seizures, organ damage and brain injury.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: [Baby L] was requiring more glucose than he would expect. Accordingly, [Dr A] wanted to boost the blood sugar levels. He
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: adopted a holding position prior to inserting a long line at 01.30 hours. We're now on to the next page and you can see the readings as they went along.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Then he changed the fluids. He discontinued the 12.5% dextrose infusion and commenced a new infusion of 15% dextrose. The fluid balance chart, of which you have a paper copy, J18033, following on from J18032, records the discontinuing of the 12.5% bag at 03.00 on the 10th and the 15% dextrose then being infused via a long line and thereafter the blood sugar figure rises to 2.9 at 11.00 and then remains between 2.7 and 2.9 until 11.00 on that day when it is 2.8.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Professor Hindmarsh says that there must have been insulin in the 12.5% bag hung at 16.30 by Belinda Williamson and Ashleigh Hudson and in the next bag of 15% dextrose hung the following day at 02.30 or 03.00 on 10 April. It was after the second 15% dextrose bag was hung at 1.45 on 11 April, later that day, that the blood sugar levels improved.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The conclusion to be drawn, say the prosecution, is that from the time of the commencement of the second 15% dextrose bag he was no longer being infused with insulin.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: At least one, and possibly two if there was a change of bags at midday on the 9th, of the 10% bags had insulin infused into them and one 15% bag was infused with insulin.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: In her evidence, the defendant accepted that the results of the blood tests prove that somebody, for no legitimate reason, put insulin into [Baby L]'s dextrose if everything had been done properly in terms of testing and that the readings on 8 April showed there was a naturally resolving hypoglycaemia that was resolved by the administration of dextrose on the 8th and it had resolved by midnight on the 8th but then, after a gap in the taking of readings, there was an exceptionally low reading and a series of low readings from 10.00 hours on the 9th.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: She also agreed that the only nursing staff in common between the shift on which [Baby F] received insulin and the shift on which [Baby L] was to receive insulin were herself and Belinda Williamson.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: She accepted the activities of Mary Griffith, [Baby L]'s designated nurse, set out on page 3 of [Baby L] and [Baby M]'s neonatal review between 9 am and 9.30, from entry 21, that she was with other children, so out of the nursery where [Baby L] and the two babies for whom the defendant was the designated nurse in that nursery, but denied that she took this as an opportunity to poison [Baby M].
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: That completes my review of [Baby L]. I will deal next with [Baby M], but we'll break now and have the ten-minute break and then continue with [Baby M] after the break.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: So [Baby M]. [Baby M] was born in good condition, crying, blue, good tone, was slow to pink up and had occasional shallow breathing. He was given five ventilation breaths at 3.5 minutes, then his sats improved, he pinked up. At 10 minutes his saturations were 93%. All this is to be found behind tile 2.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Although he was not an intensive care baby, he was placed in an incubator next to [Baby L] in nursery 1 in the top right-hand corner of the room as one enters. He too had a peripheral line inserted.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: From tile 22 onwards, between 11.13 and 12.09 that morning, there was messaging between the defendant and [Nurse A] and [Nurse E] to which you can refer for the details if you so wish.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: On the following morning, 9 April, the defendant did that extra shift -- that was the Saturday, you'll remember she volunteered to do the Saturday shift.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: [Baby M] was given antibiotics that night; tile 74.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Tile 83 sets out the staff allocation for the day shift on that Saturday, 9 April. Mary Griffith was [Baby M]'s designated nurse. He was being fed expressed breast milk via an NGT at twohourly intervals. Dr Ukoh saw [Baby M] on his morning ward round at 10.25. On examination, this is behind tile 88, he looked well and settled. He was mildly jaundiced, his abdomen was soft and normal.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Tile 91, he had a small posset with wind at 11.00.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Tile 96, timed at 12.15, Mary Griffith noted his stomach was a little distended and his work of breathing was increased.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: At 12.30, tiles 97 and 98, [Baby M]'s vital signs were recorded together with the data in the fluid balance chart by [Nurse B] because Mary Griffith had been sent on a break.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: At 14.30 hours, J18866, Mary Griffith noted that [Baby M] was to be nil by mouth because she had aspirated 1.5ml of bile before a planned feed. This stopping of enteral feeds will have been the decision of a doctor.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: [Nurse B] confirmed this and said [Baby M] was well at 14.15.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: At 15.30, an intravenous infusion of 5.3ml of 10% dextrose was set up; tile 127. J18371, the first paper document in section
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: 16, at the entry towards the middle of that sheet, records the defendant and Mary Griffith as the nurses setting up the infusion. At 15.40, the same two nurses were administering a 10% dextrose bolus to [Baby M]'s twin brother, [Baby L].
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: At tile 135, at 15.45, benzylpenicillin was administered to [Baby M]. The update in respect of that being made by both Mary Griffith and the defendant; tile 136.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Tile 137, a prescription was signed by the defendant and Mary Griffith at 15.45 for sodium chloride for [Baby M] with that being updated on the computer at that time; tile 138.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: As I reminded you when I was dealing with the evidence concerning [Baby L], Mary Griffith said that about 16.00 hours she was preparing the 12.5% dextrose infusion for [Baby L] when [Baby M]'s alarm went off. The parents had left the nursery about 10 minutes earlier.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The lights were flashing. The defendant went over to see and she said, "Yes, it's an event, it needs to be sorted".
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Mary Griffith stuck her head round the door and asked for the resuscitation call to be put out.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Ashleigh Hudson said the defendant asked her to crash bleep Dr Jayaram and she told the switchboard to put out a crash call.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: [Nurse B] said she was by the side of the defendant who administered resus breaths via a Neopuff or an Ambu bag. Although the Neopuff produced chest movements, [Baby M] wasn't breathing for himself and didn't improve. Compressions were commenced and emergency drugs were administered.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The medical staff arrived pretty promptly.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: [Nurse B] said her role was to draw up and check the resuscitation drugs. Notes were made of the drugs given and when.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: She remained at the bedside but didn't have a direct vision of [Baby M]. She was shown a piece of paper towel, exhibit PMB8, on which a number of entries were made, which corresponded to the entries in the clinical notes behind tile 171 and were of the times and the medication administered. You have a paper copy in section 16 of your second bundle.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: She recognised her writing of entries relating to doses of adrenaline given. That paper, that piece of paper, was subsequently recovered from a Morrisons bag beneath a bed in a bedroom at the defendant's home on Wednesday, 4 July 2018, as
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: was a blood gas record timed at 16.22 for [Baby M]. Mary Griffith said she had never taken any notes or readings home.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: [Nurse B] also confirmed that the rolling blood gas record reading had the information from 16.22 recorded on it. She confirmed that once the information has been placed on the rolling blood gas record, her practice was to put the original document in the confidential waste bin or the clinical waste bin, the contents of which both get incinerated. This led to the allegation put to the defendant that she must have taken that piece of paper out of the waste bin.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Belinda Williamson took over making the fluids up for [Baby L] and took no part in [Baby M]'s resuscitation.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Dr Ukoh was one of the attending clinicians. Senior house officer Dr Barrett arrived shortly after Dr Ukoh.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: She described [Baby M] as "pale and floppy and looked very, very unwell".
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Dr Ukoh's retrospectively written note of the events is behind tile 149. He was in the unit when the unusual sudden and profound apnoeic episode and cardiorespiratory arrest occurred. He described [Baby M] as "Pale +++". Cardiac massage was started. Dr Jayaram arrived at this point. His notes written at 17.40 are behind tile 210.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: By the time he arrived, three doses of adrenaline had already been given and Dr Ukoh had already intubated [Baby M] at 16.10, at which point Dr Barrett took over the task of giving chest compressions. [Baby M] was not breathing for himself, his cardiac output was not sufficient to pump blood round the body to supply the organs of his body. The entries relating to the resuscitation, which required six doses of adrenaline and other resuscitative drugs and saline, were contemporaneously recorded and he relied on the note of those details when he compiled his note.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The resuscitation took under 30 minutes and included taking over [Baby M]'s breathing following intubation and his connection to a ventilator. The readings at 16.22 were taken during the resuscitation. There was a significant metabolic acidosis of cardiorespiratory arrest and they reached a point where they were going to have to think about withdrawing support and he might not survive.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Then [Baby M] suddenly recovered. His heart rate came up and he started breathing and they could stop CPR.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Dr Jayaram said that he saw pink blotches or patches that would appear and disappear on [Baby M]'s skin and then other ones would appear and disappear. He noted them on his abdomen because that was the most obvious bit of his body that you could see because the rest of his body had people covering his chest, doing CPR. He noticed that when he got there during the start of the resuscitation.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Once circulation was restored and his heart rate came above 100, they vanished. It was very similar to what he had seen with [Baby A], whose collapse was very similar.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: He made no note of having seen it and first mentioned it in his witness statement. He said his priority at the time was dealing with the actual situation, explaining things to parents, working out his post-resuscitation care and he was thinking through things that could be going on. Infection, sepsis, hypovolaemia and pneumothorax were all issues that he addressed in the plan as set out in his notes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: He and colleagues started to say this was something different. The whole consultant body sat down two and a half months later on 29 June 2016. Someone mentioned air embolus and Dr Jayaram was prompted to do a literature search, where he found the paper to which reference has been made. The following morning, he emailed the link to colleagues because that paper described the skin discolouration that he and colleagues had seen. He had never seen anything like it before [Baby A] and has never seen it since [Baby M].
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: When cross-examined, Dr Jayaram said he told the police about seeing the discolouration when interviewed and remembered it because it was unusual but he had not appreciated the clinical significance of it at the time and that was why he didn't record it in the notes at the time.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: He disputed that failure to note it was incompetent and rejected the assertion that he did not note it because it never happened. He was dealing with the clinical situation. In retrospect, the relevance is very clear: at the time there were other things going on, other events going on. These situations are stressful and busy. He denied it was a detail that had not happened and subsequently had been added by him for some reason. He denied that that was the case.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: He agreed that shortly after the death of [Baby D] in June 2015, Dr Brearey, the neonatal lead, conducted an informal review of circumstances into the deaths that had occurred and he noticed that Lucy Letby was the nurse looking after these babies. He confirmed that he still worked with Dr Brearey and saw Dr Gibbs intermittently and saw members of staff, but said they did not
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: discuss the case. They did discuss the impact it might be having on them and they supported each other because it was extremely difficult at this time to focus on what they needed to be doing and he said that he avoided media reports.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: When interviewed on 5 July 2018, the defendant remembered [Baby M] and the day that he collapsed in some detail. He was the fifth baby in nursery 1, which usually only held four babies. Consequently, he was attached to a portable Masimo monitor and was in the corner of the nursery, which is not a usual place, and Mary Griffith was his designated nurse.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: She recalled the monitor going off when she was checking drugs with Mary Griffith. She started an airway for [Baby M] while Mary went for help. She agreed that she had co-signed for medications at 3.30 and 4.45 pm but was not sure if she administered them. She was the first at his cot side when his alarm activated.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: She denied doing anything to harm [Baby M]. She took over as his designated nurse at the resuscitation as Mary Griffith was not ITU trained. She did not know why he desaturated. She recalled it was a busy day.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: In a second interview on 12 June 2019, the following year, she confirmed she was drawing up medications when [Baby M]'s alarm sounded. In relation to the paper towel with the drug administration notes on it, PMB8, found at her home, she thought she must have taken it home inadvertently. She could think of no reason why she kept it but felt it was an error on her part, not emptying her pockets before leaving work and then inadvertently taking the note home.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: She said it may have been put to the side and forgotten about and denied that it was to remind her of an attack on [Baby M]. She was shown her diary, NAC10, and agreed that she had recorded "LD", a reference to a long day, and "twins" -- so the entry is "LD and twins" -- on 8/4/16 because she said she attended their delivery.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: She'd also entered LD extra twin days -- sorry, I'll start that again, I apologise.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: She also entered "LD, extra, twin resus" on 9 April 2016, 9/4/16, documenting this, she said, as she had done an extra shift and had documented what happened that day. The resus was a significant event.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: In the third interview on 10 November 2020, she was asked about the messages she sent at that time to Mary Griffith and [Nurse E] and the reference to the unit being in a dire way with staff.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: She said staffing concerns were readily discussed amongst nursing staff and shift leaders.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: In her evidence, the defendant said that the delivery of twins stood out in her mind because it was the first delivery she had been to where she was the allocated nurse for a baby by herself. They were very stretched that day in providing for all of the needs of the babies on the unit to make sure they were all cared for and [Baby M] wasn't in a correct space in the nursery.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Potentially, if [Baby M] had been in a proper space and they hadn't been as stretched with staff, maybe things would have been acted on quicker. He wasn't on a correct monitor and was just in a corner space, which wasn't ideal.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: She had a direct memory of this event and remembered [Nurse B] and Dr Jayaram at the resuscitation, but said there was no discolouration, anything like that described by Dr Jayaram, and no discolouration was brought to her attention.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The lighting will have been on full, but it was harder for her to assess because she was not used to caring for Asian babies, so the colour change, if any, was difficult for her to see. She did not notice any colour change. Tile 152 was her note.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: At 15.30, tile 127, she agreed she started a dextrose bag for [Baby M] with Mary Griffith, and it must have been after that, after 15.45, that the process of making up the 12.5% dextrose started. She denied that it was while Mary Griffith was getting sterile that she sabotaged [Baby M].
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: When reminded of the evidence of [Mother of Babies L & M] that it was about 10 minutes after she left the boys that a nurse called Yvonne came running up and said she had to go back and took her down in a wheelchair, she could not remember whether [Baby M]'s parents were there.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: In relation to the resuscitation notes in the Morrisons bag, she said it was common practice for such notes to be written on pieces of paper and paper towels and they went home with her in her uniform and she could not recall specifically what she did with them.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Tile 171, the blood gas readings, replicated those from the readings from the machine printout which was found under her bed in her home. She said she will have put the blood gas machine printout in her pocket to write the readings up. It was an error on her part that it didn't go in the bin. She denied she had take it out of the confidential waste bin, she had never done that, it will have gone home with the handover sheet. The notes
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: were not something that she specifically kept or had any use for. She put it under her bed because she collected paper.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: She continued to care for the twins quite frequently. She was the designated nurse for [Baby L] on the 16th, 17th, 24th and 25 April, over which time there were no adverse incidents.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: [Baby M] was discharged from hospital on 3 May. She didn't want to harm the twins, she said.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I remind you briefly of [Baby M]'s recovery after he had been resuscitated.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: [Dr A] came on duty that night and familiarised himself with the events of the afternoon. At 02.55 on 10 April, he carried out a night review of [Baby M]. His note is behind tile 300. [Baby M] was settled and had been all evening. He had no abnormal movements, his heart rate, respiratory rate and blood oxygen concentration in air were all normal. These acceptable observations were leading them towards taking him off the ventilator.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Morphine had been stopped at midnight so that he would have more respiratory effort of his own to allow him to be taken off the ventilator. He was extubated at 03.20 and put on BiPAP. At 06.00 he was moved down a step of respiratory support from BiPAP to CPAP. At 08.00 he was settled on CPAP. There was no respiratory distress and the plan was to review his progress on the ward round.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Samantha O'Brien, then a nurse in the unit, took over from the defendant as [Baby M]'s designated nurse for that night shift. She recalled the defendant describing it as a long resuscitation and told her that they had been just about to stop their efforts when they got a heart rate. She didn't recall being told why [Baby M] had collapsed. To her knowledge, it was never found out. She also confirmed that [Baby M] improved quickly during the night.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Laura Eagles said [Baby M] was in reasonably good health. There were no significant events in relation to [Baby M] on the 10th given the fact that he'd come off the ventilator quite quickly after suffering his collapse.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: [Baby M] recovered well from his collapse.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Dr Gibbs first met [Baby M] at 09.35 on 10 April and examined him. His clinical note is behind tile 348.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: There was no explanation for his cardiorespiratory arrest. He had been suffering recurrent brief bradycardias. He was on CPAP and breathing normally.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: There was an increase in carbon dioxide levels and he was a little bit acidotic. His breathing was a bit slow. A full blood count yielded normal results. His abdomen was soft and not tender.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: At 10.15, Dr Gibbs was asked by Laura Eagles to look at [Baby M] because his breathing had slowed down and stopped briefly and he had desaturated to 60%. He responded to being Neopuffed. Dr Gibbs said he made a steady recovery but on that morning, the 10th, he still wasn't behaving normally, in that he was quiet and his breathing was slow, which was explicable for a child who had very nearly died the previous afternoon, so it could have been a consequence of that that he wasn't behaving normal and had some breathing difficulties. It could also be partly the consequence of all the medication he had received to be mechanically ventilated for 10 hours or so after the cardiorespiratory arrest.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: His recovery continued and he was discharged on 3 May, by which time he was feeding well.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Other possible causes of his collapse, namely NEC, an infection or any heart defect, were excluded, and the agreed evidence of Dr Shauq, a consultant cardiologist at Alder Hey, was that Xrays confirmed that a potential issue notice by Dr Brearey of a Eustachian valve was in fact perfectly normal. So it wasn't an issue.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The agreed neurological evidence of Dr Stivaros, the lead consultant neuroradiologist at Royal Manchester Children's Hospital, was that [Baby M]'s MRI scan of his brain on 27 May 2016 at the Countess of Chester showed abnormal appearances of [Baby M]'s brain, which was most likely caused by the cardiorespiratory collapse he suffered on 9 April.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: His reading of the clinical history did not identify any other point in time when such neurological injuries are likely or even hypothetically likely to have arisen.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The imaging could not determine the underlying cause of the collapse as to which he deferred to clinical opinion.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The damage to [Baby M]'s brain is, sadly, not recoverable, and over time he may well deviate from his peers in regards to attainment and cognitive or motor function.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Professor Arthurs received six separate radiographs, the most relevant being the first dated 9 April at 17.00, tile 192. The other was dated 9 April, the same day, at 19.12, 2 hours and 12 minutes later, tile 238.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The radiographs were taken to check the line position.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The lungs were clear and the bowel gas pattern was normal and the same comments applied to the second radiograph. So there were no radiographic features of these images which could either support or refute the suggestion of an intravascular air embolus. Simply, they neither support or refute an air embolus, so there is no radiographic evidence to help you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Dr Evans, on all the evidence, concluded that [Baby M] was a preterm baby, born in good condition and, prior to his collapse, there were no concerns regarding his clinical stability. The only concern was that his feeds, his oral feeds, were discontinued at 15.00 hours because of a bilious aspirate. There was no change in heart rate or respiratory rate, so the collapse was completely unexpected and quite precipitous, so Dr Evans did not think his collapse was in any way the result of the fact that there were a couple of millilitres of aspirate from the feed, especially as oral feeds had been stopped anyway so his stomach was empty.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: He was surprised that [Baby M] did recover following a very, very robust resuscitation. This begged the question whether [Baby M] received some noxious substance prior to his arrest or whether he received a bolus of air intravenously via his long line.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: His collapse could not be explained on the basis of pneumonia or any other infection. He was able to breathe within 4 hours of his collapse. If the collapse was due to pneumonia or other lung problem, such as aspiration or infection anywhere else, he would not have expected him to make such a prompt respiratory recovery.
